questions.title: How does the producer‑consumer warp‑specialization scheme avoid deadlock in FlashAttention‑3?
questions.question_body: In Algorithm 1 the authors split a CTA into producer and consumer warpgroups and use a circular SMEM buffer with stages. I understand that producers load Q, K, V tiles while consumers compute GEMMs and softmax, but I'm confused how the synchronization (wait/notify) guarantees that no warpgroup stalls forever. Specifically, how does the "wait for the (j % s)th stage to be consumed" interact with the asynchronous TMA loads and the barrier synchronization object? Could someone walk through a concrete small example (e.g., s=2, B_r=64, B_c=64) showing the order of loads, computes, and releases?

questions.title: Why is softmax computation a bottleneck despite its low FLOP count?
questions.question_body: The paper states that the exponential unit on H100 provides only ~3.9 TFLOPS while FP16 matmul offers ~989 TFLOPS, leading to softmax taking up to 50% of cycle time. However, softmax only processes N² values which seems negligible compared to the GEMM work. Can someone explain why the hardware throughput disparity makes softmax a bottleneck in practice, and how the ping‑pong scheduling mitigates this issue?

questions.title: What are the exact layout constraints for FP8 WGMMA operands and how does the in‑kernel transpose satisfy them?
questions.question_body:
Section 4.2 says FP8 WGMMA only accepts k‑major operand layout, while Q, K, V are stored contiguously in the head‑dimension. The authors propose an in‑kernel transpose using LDSM/STSM instructions. I am unclear on:
1) What does "k‑major" mean for a tile of V in memory?
2) How does loading a tile with LDSM/STSM change its layout from mn‑major to k‑major?
3) Why is an additional register permutation needed after the first GEMM accumulator before the second GEMM? A step‑by‑step description of these transformations would help.

questions.title: How does block quantization reduce FP8 quantization error compared to per‑tensor scaling?
questions.question_body: The paper reports a 2.6× accuracy improvement for FP8 FlashAttention‑3 using block quantization. I understand per‑tensor scaling keeps a single scale factor for an entire Q/K/V matrix, but I'm not sure why splitting into blocks (e.g., B_r×d) helps with outliers. Does each block get its own exponent bias? How is the scaling factor computed per block without incurring extra memory bandwidth? Also, how does this interact with the subsequent softmax rescaling step?

questions.title: Why does incoherent processing (random orthogonal transform) not affect attention output?
questions.question_body: In Section 4.2 the authors multiply Q and K by a random orthogonal matrix M before FP8 quantization, claiming that (Q M)(K M)^T = QK^T. I see that M M^T = I, but I am worried about numerical issues: does applying M change the distribution of values such that quantization error is reduced uniformly? How is M generated efficiently (they mention diagonal +/-1 and Hadamard), and does this extra multiplication cost affect performance?

questions.title: How is the 2‑stage GEMM‑softmax pipeline implemented without violating data dependencies?
questions.question_body: Algorithm 2 shows overlapping of two WGMMA calls with softmax of the next block. The pseudocode mentions "commit but do not wait" for the first GEMM while softmax for the previous block proceeds. In practice, how are CUDA barriers or warp synchronizations used to enforce that the softmax uses only completed S_cur and that O_i accumulation uses only ready \tilde{P}_cur? Are there hidden dependencies that could cause race conditions on registers or shared memory?

questions.title: What limits prevent FlashAttention‑3 from achieving >80% utilization on H100 like cuDNN GEMM kernels?
questions.question_body: The authors note that FlashAttention‑2 gets only ~35% utilization on H100 and FlashAttention‑3 improves to ~75%. Yet cuDNN GEMM reaches 80–90%. Is the remaining gap due to kernel launch overhead, register pressure from pipelining, or inherent algorithmic constraints (e.g., needing to keep intermediate results in FP32)? Any insight into what parts of FlashAttention‑3 could be further optimized would be helpful.

questions.title: How is numerical error measured for FP8 FlashAttention‑3 and why is RMSE used?
questions.question_body: Section 6.3 compares RMSE against an FP64 reference on synthetic data with outliers. I'm unclear whether RMSE is computed on the final output O or also on intermediate matrices like S or P. Also, does keeping softmax accumulators in FP32 affect this metric? Would another metric such as max absolute error give a different picture of where errors are introduced?

questions.title: Can FlashAttention‑3’s techniques be applied to other attention variants like sparse or local attention?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions multi‑query and grouped query attention but not sparse patterns (e.g., BigBird) or sliding window attention. Since these variants modify the shape of K/V accessed per query block, would the producer–consumer asynchrony and block quantization still work unchanged, or are there extra challenges (e.g., irregular memory accesses) that prevent straightforward adaptation?

questions.title: What are the trade‑offs between a 2‑stage and a 3‑stage pipeline in FlashAttention‑3?
questions.question_body: The authors briefly discuss a possible 3‑stage extension that would overlap another GEMM with softmax but require more registers. Could someone elaborate on how adding a third stage changes the instruction schedule and memory usage? Is there empirical evidence that beyond a certain sequence length or head dimension the extra overlap yields diminishing returns?
